---
title: "Limitations"
description: "The honest account of what oboro misses, and why reading the sanitised output is part of the workflow rather than an optional extra."
---

This page is the honest account.
A privacy tool that oversells itself is worse than none, because it replaces caution with confidence.

::: {.callout-warning}

## Read the output before you send it

Every limitation below has the same mitigation.
The sanitised file is a few seconds' reading, and that reading is part of the workflow rather than an optional extra.

:::

## The model cannot tell a name from a phrase

This is the sharpest limitation, and it is not something a better setting fixes.

Measured on the shipped model:

| Text | Score |
| --- | --- |
| `Thomas Bernard`, inside a document | 0.237 |
| `The quick brown fox` | 0.218 |

They are eighteen thousandths apart.
No threshold separates a real name from an ordinary phrase, so the tool redacts both and expects you to put back what it got wrong.

That is why [`oboro review`](reference.qmd#review) exists.

Two consequences follow.
Ordinary prose sometimes comes back with holes in it, which is a nuisance.
And a name may still be missed, which is not.

## Context changes what the model sees

The same name scores 0.47 alone and 0.24 once surrounded by a document.

The default threshold is calibrated on whole documents for exactly this reason.
An earlier version was tuned on single sentences and silently missed a name in a real file, which is the failure this tool exists to prevent.

## Identifiers that fail their own checksum are not found

A mistyped IBAN, a SIREN with a digit dropped, a card number that fails Luhn: none are detected.

The check is what makes the rules trustworthy rather than noisy, so it stays.
Add a [custom pattern](configuration.qmd#patterns) if your documents carry identifiers that do not validate.

## Some scanned PDFs are still refused

A PDF whose pages are images yields almost no text.
On a build with `--features ocr` the images on those pages are read instead, which covers what a scanner produces: one image per page.

Three kinds are still refused rather than half read, each naming the page.

Pages whose image uses a codec that cannot be handed to the recogniser.
Only `DCTDecode`, `JPXDecode` and `CCITTFaxDecode` are read, so `JBIG2Decode` is refused, and so is a `FlateDecode` page image of the kind Ghostscript and other re-encoding pipelines produce.
A fax image with `/EncodedByteAlign` set is refused for the same reason: it cannot be described to the recogniser, and describing it wrongly would recognise noise.

Pages whose image is wrapped in another filter, such as `[/FlateDecode /DCTDecode]`.
The stream is stored as the document holds it, so the codec is still under a layer this does not unwrap.

Pages holding no image at all, where the text was drawn as vector shapes.
Nothing is embedded to recognise, and rasterising the page needs a large external library the tool does not carry.
A page whose only images are too small to be a scan, such as a rule or a spacer, is refused the same way and says so.

A scan drawn through a form XObject rather than placed on the page directly is found, so that shape is read rather than refused.

Both the decision and the refusal are per page.
A page short of text is read as a scan whatever the pages around it hold, so a scanned page in an otherwise textual PDF is recognised rather than carried along by the text on the others.
One unreadable page refuses the whole file rather than dropping out of it silently.

Two pages are kept rather than refused, both deliberately.

A page carrying a few words and no image, such as a section divider or a continuation sheet.
Demanding an image of one would refuse documents that read perfectly well.

A page whose image yields no text.
A blank page is ordinary in a scan and nothing distinguishes it from a page too faint to read.
That second one is the gap worth knowing about: a page whose writing is too faint contributes nothing, and the document still comes back as read.

Without `--features ocr` a page short of text is refused, and the error says so.

## A PDF page can be read short without anything saying so

A page that cannot be processed at all is caught: the extractor stops there, `oboro` notices the document came back shorter than its page count and refuses it, naming the page.

A page read *incompletely* is not caught, and cannot be.
The extractor drops text it does not recognise the shape of rather than failing on it: a `Tj` operand that is not a string is skipped, as are surrogate-range code units.
The page still comes back, just with less on it than it holds, and nothing distinguishes that from a page which really did say less.

The per-page floor catches the worst of it, since a page reduced to almost nothing is then read as a scan.
A page that loses a line or two stays above the floor and is used as it is, so a value in that line is neither redacted nor reported.

This is the one place where output can be short of the input without an error, so a PDF whose text matters is worth reading over before you send it.

## Formats it does not read

Older `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt` are not read at all, nor are the OpenDocument
text, spreadsheet and presentation formats, `.odt`, `.ods` and `.odp`.
Neither is anything embedded inside a document: a spreadsheet pasted into a Word file is not reached.

Inside a `.pptx`, a footer set through PowerPoint's Header and Footer dialog
is written into the slide master and the layouts rather than the slides
themselves, so it is not read; a client name or a confidentiality line set
there once is missed.
A chart's cached category labels, under `ppt/charts/`, are visible on the
slide and are not read either.
`SmartArt` is read, because the `mc:Fallback` inside the slide carries its
shapes and their runs.

## Recognition accuracy on real scans is not guaranteed

The tests read rendered text at a generous size, for a plain image and for both PDF codecs, and check three things: that none of the planted values survive cleaning, that two of the six rendered lines come back from recognition rather than being lost on the way in, and that the provider name restores.
That covers the path end to end, not the conditions a real scan arrives in, and two lines out of six is a long way from measuring how much of a page was recognised.

A photograph taken at an angle, a low resolution fax or a handwritten note is another matter.
Treat text recovered from images as less reliable than text read directly, and check the output before sharing it.

## The hook does not cover what you type

The hooks clean what a tool hands the model and put values back into what the model writes.
What you type yourself is never touched.

This is not an omission to be fixed later.
The event that fires on a prompt, `UserPromptSubmit`, can add context to a prompt; it cannot rewrite the prompt.
There is nowhere for Oboro to stand between your keyboard and the model, so a value pasted into the chat reaches the model as you typed it.

File content and command output are covered.
Your own words are not, in any tool, by any configuration.

Paste a document rather than retyping its contents, and the hook covers it.

## What redaction does not hide

Replacing a name with `[[PERSON_1]]` removes the name.
It does not remove the shape of the story around it.

A document describing a dispute with a named supplier in a named town in a named month may identify everyone involved even with every name replaced.
Structured identifiers are the part this tool can handle; inference from context is not, and no placeholder scheme solves it.

## Languages

Detection does not depend on the document's language, and you never declare one.
Structured identifiers such as emails, IBANs, payment cards and IP addresses are matched by format, so they work in any language.
The recognition model is multilingual and reads the whole document in one pass, so a file that mixes languages, for example French and English names side by side, is handled at once with no per-language setting.

Street addresses are matched by shape too, in the three word orders languages use: the type before the name (`12 rue de la Paix`, `3 via Roma`), after it (`10 Downing Street`), or welded onto it (`Hauptstraße 5`).
An address whose street type is not in that vocabulary is left to the recognition model or to your denylist.

Two gaps in the postcode patterns are worth knowing.

A postcode of four bare digits followed by a place name, as in Belgium, Switzerland, Austria and Scandinavia, is deliberately not matched: it cannot be told apart from `2024 January`, and matching it would put a hole in every document that mentions a year.
Those addresses are still caught when the street line is, and the postcode alone is rarely identifying.

Five-digit, British, Canadian, Dutch and American postcodes are matched.
Anything else is not.

Two settings exist as hints, and neither is required.
[`regions`](configuration.qmd#regions) widens which national phone number formats are read, and a number in international `+` form is read whatever it holds.
[`ocr_languages`](configuration.qmd#ocr_languages) names what an image is written in, and left unset the installed trained data is used.

The tool has been exercised mostly on French and English, though nothing in it is limited to those two.
